Raucous

RAW-kus -- from Latin raucus ('hoarse, harsh-sounding'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Raucous is making a harsh, loud noise; disorderly and boisterous.

The comedy club's Friday crowd was always the most raucous of the week, howling with laughter at every punchline.

Worked Example

By midnight, the reunion had turned genuinely raucous, with three different conversations shouted over a blaring playlist.

That loud, disorderly, high-energy noise -- the kind that makes it hard to hear anything else -- is exactly what raucous describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

boisterous: noisy and full of rowdy energy

deafening: so loud it overwhelms the ears

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hushed: very quiet and subdued

serene: peacefully calm and quiet

Where it sits · how overpowering the noise gets — boisterous → raucous → deafening

boisterous vs. raucous: Boisterous is milder than raucous: kids get boisterous after birthday cake, while a raucous crowd is harsher and louder — a grating roar that fills the whole room.

deafening vs. raucous: Deafening is stronger than raucous: a raucous party is harsh and loud, but a deafening jet engine goes further — so overwhelming that ground crews wear heavy ear protection.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Raucous traces back to Latin raucus, 'hoarse, harsh-sounding' -- but that root doesn't extend cleanly into other common modern English words, so raucous is best learned as a strong, standalone word for loud, disorderly noise.

Use the root in a new word: raucously

Use the root in a new word: raucously: The whole bar cheered raucously the moment the underdog team scored.

Word Building

Word Choice

Raucous almost always describes sound -- a raucous crowd, a raucous party, a raucous laugh -- loud, disorderly, and full of energy, whether the tone is celebratory or simply chaotic.
